definition: Myopic means lacking foresight; focused only on the short term.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word myopic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know myopic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Skipping breakfast to cram five more vocabulary words is myopic — the gain shows up now, the blur arrives by the second hour of the exam.
A narrow view leaves things out to the sides; a myopic one loses everything past the near term.
Blind goes past myopic — the nearsighted planner still sees this quarter clearly; the blind one sees nothing coming from any distance.

Shortsighted is the plain-English twin of myopic: both name the trade of far costs for near gains. The difference is register, not meaning — shortsighted scolds in everyday clothes, while myopic is the critic's word, at home in editorials about policies, budgets, and strategies.

Blinkered borrows the racehorse's eye-shields: unable to see outside one narrow view, deaf to other perspectives and inconvenient facts. Myopic runs along a different axis — time. A myopic planner may weigh every viewpoint in the room and still trade next year away for next month.

Myopic means lacking foresight; focused only on the short term.
The eighty-dollar roof patch waited all autumn.

There was always a nearer use for eighty dollars — a concert, a brake light, a weekend — and the stain on the ceiling grew politely, an inch a month, until a February thaw brought the bedroom ceiling down.
The contractor's bill was four thousand dollars.
Every myopic decision along the way had felt, at the time, like thrift.
Myopic is the exact word because each choice lacked foresight — focused only on the short term, the word's borrowed meaning from nearsightedness: near things sharp, far things blurred.
A myopic decision isn't stupid and isn't reckless; next month simply crowds next year out of focus.
The bill for the far blur always arrives.
Myopic is the critic's word for decisions that can't see past the near term — policies, budgets, strategies.
It is not stupidity: this unit's inept fails for lack of skill, but a myopic plan may be executed brilliantly toward a horizon two feet away.
Its true opposite in this unit is judicious, which weighs the far term as heavily as the near.
Shortsighted says the same thing in plainer clothes.

When Averline Motors posted record quarterly profits, the business press noticed a line item: the company had eliminated its apprenticeship program to get there.
The savings were real — four million dollars a year, straight to the bottom line.
An industry columnist called the move myopic.
The apprentices had been the pipeline: nearly every master machinist on the floor had come up through the program over twenty years.
The company would look brilliant, she wrote, for exactly as long as the current machinists stayed.
Retirements would arrive on schedule; replacements would not.
Five years later Averline was paying triple wages to poach machinists from rivals — and training them on arrival anyway.
